findings.title: Findings converge on the projection-freshness signal (D8's in-memory, live-seam-only lag)
findings.why_it_matters: Four findings from both critics reach one mechanism from different directions. D8 computes freshness as an in-memory monotonic timestamp exposed only on `/telemetry/status` and the web UI banner. Every other reader gets no freshness signal. Finding 3: `/health` and `/api/apps` (which hass-hassette and `hassette status` poll) keep reporting `ok`/running after the projector wedges. Finding 11: a crashed session's per-app rows read as RUNNING. Finding 12: a stopped session's stored `/health` status reads as current in snapshot mode. Finding 13: `as_of` comes from a heartbeat that a seed, or a `DatabaseService` loop independent of the projector, wrote. Each finding proposes its own read-time rule (a live-mode `/health` downgrade, a crashed-session render rule, a forced snapshot `degraded`, a seed `stopped_at` stamp). D8's own deciding factor says the system must never show confident stale status, and every one of these consumers does. The question is whether the freshness signal should be redesigned, or even moved to a different layer, instead of patched four times. One possibility is a persisted fact that every reader applies in the one place runtime rows join to their session.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the projection-freshness mechanism before addressing Findings 3, 11, 12 and 13 individually. Open questions: is freshness in-memory or persisted; which clock defines it (projector run, write commit, heartbeat); is it applied at read time in one shared place or per route; does it reach `/health`, `/api/apps`, snapshots and released clients; how does it relate to `as_of` and to D15's "process state unknown" label; and is a separate freshness signal needed at all once those questions are answered.
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the projection-freshness mechanism before addressing Findings 3, 11, 12 and 13 individually.

findings.title: Findings converge on D19's issue cut for wire and consumer changes (the `/health` and WS `connected` rewrite)
findings.why_it_matters: Four contract-caller findings come down to how D19 spreads edits to `SystemStatusResponse` and `ConnectedData` across issues and releases. Finding 4: required fields are removed outright, which breaks released clients and the client-compat gate. Finding 5: a new `/health` start-time field has no name and no issue. Finding 6: issue 8 can land before the `/health` field it reads, and `/health` is edited in #2806, issue 7, issue 8 and issue 9. Finding 14: `connected` drops required fields that stale browser bundles still validate against. Each proposes its own sequencing patch. D12's own deciding factor is "rewrite `SystemStatusResponse` once", yet D9, D13, D14 and D15 each change it in a different D19 row. The question is whether D19's cut should be re-evaluated as a whole for these wire surfaces, rather than adding a dependency edge here and a defaulted field there. The operational-resilience critic did not reach D19. This convergence rests on one critic plus the ledger's own D12.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate D19's issue cut for the wire and consumer changes before addressing Findings 4, 5, 6 and 14 individually. Open questions: how many issues touch `SystemStatusResponse` and `ConnectedData`, and in what order relative to #2806; whether removals are staged across releases or coordinated with a hass-hassette release; which issue owns the new `/health` start-time field and its consumers; where seed runtime rows and the generator's `WebContext` adoption land relative to the route switches; and whether issue 5 changes any WS message shape.
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate D19's issue cut for the wire and consumer changes before addressing Findings 4, 5, 6 and 14 individually.
findings.choice_reason: Multiple PRs can land on main before a release; breakage only reaches users at release; each PR must pass CI.

findings.title: Projection freshness is not persisted or exposed; `/health`, `/api/apps`, `as_of` and snapshots read a wedged projector as healthy
findings.why_it_matters: After D9, `/health` `status`, `websocket_connected` and `services`, plus `/api/apps` statuses, are the last committed projection. D8 puts the staleness signal only on `/telemetry/status` and the web-UI banner. hass-hassette polls only `get_health()` and `get_apps()` (coordinator.py:99-103), and `hassette status` reads `/health`. So a wedged projector or a failing write path leaves `/health` at `status: ok` with HTTP 200, and `/api/apps` showing running apps, indefinitely. D15's `as_of` comes from `last_heartbeat_at`, which `DatabaseService` writes independently of the projector (D3 splits them), so a dead projector with a live heartbeat gives a current-looking `as_of` over stale rows. D8's "last successful write" also needs one sentence of precision. D1.2 reads the snapshot inside the job, so every run submits a job, including no-op runs. The ledger should state that a no-op run counts, so lag doesn't grow in an idle, healthy system. Both critics proposed persisting `projected_at` per session. The contract critic also proposed a read-time `degraded` downgrade on live `/health`, and explicitly rejected a 503, which would flip Docker probes and hass-hassette to unhealthy over a display lag.
findings.recommended: A: Persist `projected_at` per session (updated by every successful run, including no-ops, in the same transaction). Use it for `as_of` and for lag in both modes, expose it on `/health`, and have live-mode `/health` downgrade `status` to `degraded` in-band (never 503) when lag exceeds the banner threshold.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Removing required `uptime_seconds` / `entity_count` from `/health` breaks the released client, hass-hassette, and the repo's client-compat gate
findings.why_it_matters: `SystemStatusResponse.uptime_seconds` and `entity_count` are required with no default. Lenient parsing absorbs unknown fields and enum values but not missing required ones (`errors.py:84`), so released clients raise `ResponseValidationError`. hass-hassette pins `hassette-client==0.56.0` and maps that error to a poll error (coordinator.py:117-123). After this change every installed integration's entities go unavailable until hass-hassette ships against a new client, and `check_server_version` only guards new-client/old-server. The repo's own `client_compat` check types fixtures by the newest published release reachable from HEAD, so `GET /api/health` fails on the PR, and that check has no deliberate-break escape. `check_wire_compat.py` also blocks `response-required-property-removed` unless `tools/wire_compat_ignore.txt` gets lines. D14 mentions only `feat!:` plus a footer. This would be the first required-field removal from `/health`. #2806 removes only defaulted fields.
findings.recommended: A: Two-step removal. Defaulted fields in release N, deleted in N+1, with the ordering stated in D19.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 2

findings.title: D13 relies on a `/health` start-time field that no decision defines, and `/health` `uptime_seconds`'s fate is unspecified
findings.why_it_matters: D13 says since-restart "reads the current session's `started_at` from `/health`", but `SystemStatusResponse` has no such field. D9 lists exactly what it writes, with no start time, and D15 adds only `mode`/`as_of`. The field the frontend keys its whole since-restart window on has no name, type, or owner issue. The CLI renders `/health.uptime_seconds` through `CliFormat("uptime")` and the docs cite it. Whether `/health` keeps `uptime_seconds` is not stated. Computing "now minus `started_at`" is wrong for a stopped session in snapshot mode, and a persisted value is stale.
findings.recommended: A: Add `session_started_at` to `/health`, in the same D19 issue as the frontend change that consumes it, and keep `uptime_seconds` as a live-only value.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 2

findings.title: D19 leaves main in states where wire, frontend, generator and seeds disagree
findings.why_it_matters: Each issue squash-merges to main, from which releases ship. (1) Issue 8 depends only on 5 but reads the `/health` start time that issue 7 adds. If 8 lands first, `use-scoped-query.ts:76` keeps `waitingForUptime` true and since-restart queries never fetch. Issue 8 also carries D14's `entity_count` removal, in an unordered series with #2806 and issue 7 editing the same response. (2) Issue 5 "moves the `apps_changed` broadcast" and emits payload-free invalidations, but the frontend overlay that consumes payload messages is removed only in issue 8. The ledger doesn't say issue 5 keeps today's message shapes. (3) Issue 4 changes `create_fastapi_app`, which the compat-fixture generator, `web_api_service.py`, the schema export, and many tests call, but the generator switch is assigned to issue 9. (4) Issues 6 and 7 switch reads to runtime tables while the seed scenarios that write runtime rows land in issue 9, so client-compat generation (the `empty` coverage gap), e2e, and demo seeds return empty data in between.
findings.recommended: A: Re-cut D19's dependencies and scope as described.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 2

findings.title: Log persistence can starve the projector's awaited `submit()`, and D8 has no remedy
findings.why_it_matters: Log batches use `enqueue()` → `put_nowait`, and the projector uses `submit()` → `await queue.put(...)` on the same 2000-slot queue. `asyncio.Queue.put_nowait` checks only `full()`, not waiting putters. When the worker frees a slot it wakes the first waiting putter via a scheduled callback, and a log flush (`call_soon_threadsafe`) that runs first takes the slot. Under a sustained storm (an app in an error loop), the projector's `put` can wait out its whole deadline. With a per-attempt timeout under 30s, every attempt fails, lag passes the banner threshold, and the UI goes degraded because of the storm, whose own ERROR logs feed the same queue. The heartbeat shares the exposure, so a storm also walks `DatabaseService` toward its 3-strike restart. D8 framed contention as an unmeasured latency risk, but this is a starvation mechanism.
findings.recommended: B: Have `enqueue()` treat waiting `submit()` putters as "full" (drop and count), so awaited writes always get the next free slot.
findings.chosen: B: Have `enqueue()` treat waiting `submit()` putters as "full" (drop and count), so awaited writes always get the next free slot.

findings.title: A timed-out projector write may still commit; the in-memory baseline and DB disagree and history rows duplicate
findings.why_it_matters: D1.3 diffs against the "last committed snapshot" and D8 wraps each attempt in its own timeout. `submit()` documents that a started write "may commit", and that a caller bounding it with its own timeout gets no outcome. If the projector's timeout fires after the worker starts the job, the transaction (including `app_status_events` rows) may commit while the projector treats it as failed, keeps the baseline, and the next run appends the same history rows again. That leaves permanent duplicated lifecycle history. Because all jobs serialize on the single writer, the job itself is the only party that knows the outcome.
findings.chosen: Add to D1 item 3: "The baseline is advanced by the write job itself, immediately after its commit, never by the projector task from the result of its await. Jobs serialize on the single writer, so the next job always diffs against what actually committed, and a timed-out attempt needs no reconciliation."

findings.title: Failed projector writes retry with no backoff, and each failure logs back into the failing path
findings.why_it_matters: D1.7 says a failed job "leaves its keys dirty; the next run, or at latest the next resync, rewrites them". With the DB full, locked or the queue wedged, the projector may retry every debounce (~250ms) plus the attempt timeout, logging an ERROR each time. Those ERRORs are persisted through the same write queue (`logging_.py`), so the projector's failure feeds the queue it is failing on. The ledger doesn't say whether a dirty key left by a failure schedules an immediate re-run, and states no backoff, rate limit, or log deduplication on a write path whose blast radius is now the whole UI. Classified User-directed because the fix adds state (a backoff timer and a failing/recovered flag).
findings.recommended: A: Exponential backoff with transition-only logging, and the lag banner as the steady-state signal.
findings.chosen: A: Exponential backoff with transition-only logging, and the lag banner as the steady-state signal.

findings.title: D7's final write has no owner, no dirty marks, no budget, and no durable failure signal
findings.why_it_matters: (1) `Hassette.before_shutdown` calls `self._bus.remove_all_listeners()` first, so the projector's subscription is gone before children stop, and shutdown transitions mark nothing dirty. The final run must be an unconditional mark-all, which the ledger doesn't say. (2) At final-run time the registry is mid-teardown, and D1.6 says what not to infer but not what a stopped app's row should say. (3) The final wave gets about a second of shutdown budget, `drain_write_queue` is capped, and the run may wait behind a deep queue. If the budget lapses, `_force_terminal` skips `on_shutdown`. (4) "Counted and logged" is unobservable: the count dies with the process, and the ERROR log goes through persistence whose queue is detaching. (5) `_do_finalize_session` already catches and logs every exception, and D7 moves it later without saying it stops swallowing. (6) The only hook that sits "before DB detach" without new ordering is `DatabaseService.on_shutdown`, which would have to call up into the projector.
findings.recommended: A: Pin the owner as a `Resource` child with `depends_on`, mark-all on the final run, a bounded budget from the final wave, a durable non-DB failure signal, and finalization that no longer swallows.
findings.chosen: A: Pin the owner as a `Resource` child with `depends_on`, mark-all on the final run, a bounded budget from the final wave, a durable non-DB failure signal, and finalization that no longer swallows.
findings.choice_reason: Applied with a corrected edge: CommandExecutor depends on the projector so it flushes first (dependents shut down first).

findings.title: Rows of a crashed or force-terminated session read as confidently "running"
findings.why_it_matters: On crash, OOM kill or force-terminal there is no final write, so the session's `app_runtime` rows keep their last projected status (RUNNING). Only the `sessions` row is repaired, and only at the next startup (`_do_mark_orphaned_sessions`). D15 labels the session "process state unknown", but per-app rows carry no qualifier, and D6's "latest session" fallback in snapshot mode serves exactly this case.
findings.recommended: A: Add the read-time "last known" rule at the session join.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: In snapshot mode `/health` serves the stored `status` / `websocket_connected` as if current
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a snapshot served to something other than the Vite UI (CLI via `HASSETTE_URL`, or the released client). D4 makes snapshot mode dev-only, so this only matters if someone points a client at it. D7 stores the true final state and D9 stores `system_status` computed in-process, so a cleanly stopped session's `/health` reports `ok`, `websocket_connected: true`, and running services. `SystemHealthStatus` has no "stopped" value. The only signals are the new `mode`/`as_of` fields, which a released client ignores as unknown, so a CLI pointed at a snapshot sees a healthy live system. That contradicts D15's deciding factor.
findings.recommended: A: Force `degraded`/`false` in the snapshot read branch.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: "Latest session" is undefined for snapshot reads, and seed `as_of` comes from a generator-written heartbeat
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: more than one `sessions` row with null `stopped_at` (crash then restart, which the design anticipates in D15's "process state unknown" label). D6 tells live mode its session, while snapshot mode falls back to "the latest session" by an unstated rule (max `started_at`? max id?). D15's `as_of` is that session's `stopped_at` or `last_heartbeat_at`. For a seed, the heartbeat is whatever the generator wrote, so a seed with null `stopped_at` is labeled "process state unknown" and `as_of` is inferred from a generated heartbeat. Readers infer the age of the data from a value no process produced.
findings.recommended: A: Define the shared latest-session query and have `serve_seed.py` stamp `stopped_at`.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Payload-free `app_status_changed` / `service_status` shapes are undefined, and `connected` losing required fields silently disables the "server updated" banner in open tabs
findings.why_it_matters: (1) "Payload-free invalidations of the queries that read the affected data" can't target anything without a key, and a keyless message duplicates the existing `apps_changed`. `AppStatusChangedData` requires `status`, so any reduction is a wire model, `ws-schema.json` and generated validator change, and the ledger doesn't say which fields remain. (2) `ConnectedData` requires `uptime_seconds`, `entity_count` and `app_count`, enforced by the generated validator. A tab running the old bundle after a server upgrade, the exact case `isVersionChange`/`serverUpdated` exist for, gets a `connected` that fails validation. `use-websocket.ts:96-99` logs and returns, the reconnect invalidate-all and `handleWsConnected` never run, and the "reload" prompt never appears.
findings.recommended: A: Keyed reduced messages, plus optional-then-remove for `ConnectedData`.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 2

findings.title: A 30s heartbeat cuts tolerance to writer occupancy from about 15 minutes to about 90 seconds
findings.why_it_matters: `max_consecutive_heartbeat_failures=3` at 300s tolerates about 15 minutes of an unresponsive writer before `serve()` raises and `DatabaseService` restarts. At 30s, three strikes tolerate about 90s. Retention is one fire-and-forget job (`enqueue_if_ready(self._do_run_retention_cleanup)`) that loops up to 100 batches × 1000 rows per target while holding the single writer, and the size failsafe is another. A large first retention pass after upgrade, a size-failsafe drain, or a log storm (Finding 7) can plausibly produce three strikes. In the new design a restart also closes the read connection that every GET route now depends on (Finding 16). D3 says the constants are "re-derived" but no derivation exists when a legitimate maintenance job can outlast any timeout under 30s. Today's constant comment sizes the 30s timeout against a 300s interval.
findings.chosen: A: Progress-based strikes.
findings.choice_reason: Applied with a corrected progress signal: a write-progress counter bumped per job completion and per maintenance batch commit, since retention is one long job.

findings.title: Required DB plus all-reads-from-DB turns a `DatabaseService` restart into a full-UI outage with no stated degraded behavior
findings.why_it_matters: Before this change a DB restart cost only the telemetry tabs. Afterwards `read_db` raises `RuntimeError` from `on_shutdown`/`_force_terminal` until `on_initialize` finishes again, so `/health`, `/apps` and every WS-triggered refetch fail together, while the live-seam `/telemetry/status` still answers. The ledger doesn't say what the UI shows during the restart window. It also doesn't address restart-budget exhaustion (3 per 120s, TRANSIENT): the apps keep running while the UI stays blank permanently. D1.8 protects app start from a slow DB, but nothing protects the operator's view.
findings.recommended: A: State the DB-unavailable UI contract, probe behavior, and cached-read allowance.
findings.chosen: A: State the DB-unavailable UI contract, probe behavior, and cached-read allowance.

findings.title: `TelemetryStatusResponse` can't express "unavailable" counters without breaking released parsers, and projector degradation's HTTP status is unspecified
findings.why_it_matters: The counters are `int = 0`. D8's "unavailable, not zeros" most naturally encodes as `null`, which a released client parsing into `int` rejects with `ResponseValidationError`, and this probe path is parsed with `status_model_on_503=True`. D8 also says a never-succeeded projector "reports degraded". On this route, `degraded: true` currently always comes with HTTP 503 ("A probe ... the CLI and container health checks read it as data"), so a projector problem would read as a database outage to container health checks. The ledger doesn't say whether projector degradation maps to 503 or stays in-band. Classified User-directed because the 503 question changes probe behavior.
findings.recommended: A: Additive defaulted fields; projector degradation never changes this probe's HTTP status.
findings.chosen: Reconsider all ad hoc counters together: one (stage, reason) counter registry persisted as session_counters rows and read from the DB (new D24); counters leave /telemetry/status, zero-fallback deleted.
findings.choice_reason: User asked which counters these were, then asked to treat them with the other ad hoc counters that have piled up.

findings.title: Snapshot mode has no WebSocket, but the frontend infers liveness from its socket and D15 never defines `/api/ws` in snapshot mode
findings.why_it_matters: `overview-tab.tsx:91-97` dims the overview when `connection !== "connected"`. `system-health.tsx` renders the dot and an "unreachable" hint keyed to the socket, and `use-websocket.ts` retries forever. With `live=None` there is no WS broadcast, so the Done-when render ("with a snapshot banner") would show a dimmed overview, a red connection dot, and a retry loop. D15 names `/health.mode` as the signal but never says the connection UI consumes it, or what `/api/ws` does in snapshot mode. This is a missing behavior that D15's deciding factor implies.
findings.chosen: Add to D15: "In snapshot mode `/api/ws` is not mounted (404). The frontend does not open a socket when `/health.mode === "snapshot"`, and connection-dependent UI (overview dimming, the connection dot, the unreachable hint) derives its state as `mode === "snapshot" ? "snapshot" : wsState`, never from socket absence alone."

findings.title: The new `snapshot_mode` problem code trips client and compat-coverage gates that issue 9 doesn't list
findings.why_it_matters: Every `ProblemCode` must be in exactly one of `GENERIC_CODES` or `CODE_ERRORS`, or the client's tests fail. `tools/client_compat_coverage.py` fails generation when a `ProblemCode` has no request that answers it, and per D10 the generator always passes a fake `LiveSeam`, so no fixture can produce `snapshot_mode`. Released clients resolve the unknown code by status to `ConflictError`, the same class as retry-later codes, which D15 says callers shouldn't retry. None of this is in D19 issue 9.
findings.chosen: Add to D19 issue 9's scope: classify `snapshot_mode` in the client (a non-retryable class in `CODE_ERRORS`, or `GENERIC_CODES`); handle compat coverage (an `EXCLUDED` entry with its reason, or a `live=None` stub variant); and document the code as non-retryable on its `ProblemCode` docstring.

findings.title: D18's sizing assumption ignores counter rows that change on every handler invocation
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: users with hundreds of listeners/jobs per session (a framework with unknown external apps; the ledger itself says in-repo usage is not evidence of demand). D6/D17 put listener and job guard counters in per-session tables that the projector rewrites. A busy listener's counter changes continuously, so after any activity every resync rewrites every active listener/job row, and the "tens of rows" argument doesn't hold for counters. The ~1,000-row revisit threshold is a read-the-logs trigger, and nothing emits row counts per run.
findings.recommended: B: Emit per-run changed-row count and duration now; chunk only when it shows up.
findings.chosen: D: Rewrite D18 honestly: measured costs, D8 lag-degrade as the automatic backstop, write volume named as the scaling cost.
findings.choice_reason: User: a log-based trigger isn't observable automatically; it relies on someone seeing and reporting it.

findings.title: Payload-free WS invalidations lose their only delivery guarantee on WS reconnect
